keyVerseText: But he said, Nay; lest while ye gather up the tares, ye root up also the wheat with them.
rootMeaning: The Greek adverb ἅμα (háma) is a primary particle that fundamentally conveys the idea of simultaneity or close association, meaning 'at the same time' or 'together.' Its root sense emphasizes an inseparable joining or concurrence of actions or entities rather than merely a sequential or additive relationship. This nuance enriches the common English glosses like 'together' or 'with' by highlighting a unity or immediacy in timing or relationship that goes beyond simple accompaniment.
usageInScripture: With a total of ten occurrences, ἅμα is consistently used as an adverb or preposition denoting actions or entities occurring simultaneously or closely associated. It is translated variously as 'together,' 'withal,' 'with,' 'also,' and even 'early in the morning,' showing flexibility but always retaining the core sense of concurrence or unity. This range of translations reveals that the word functions both temporally and relationally, emphasizing either simultaneous timing or intimate association depending on context.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding ἅμα deepens our grasp of the interconnectedness and unity portrayed in Scripture, reflecting how God’s work and presence often operate in harmony and immediacy. The word’s emphasis on 'togetherness' or 'at the same time' can remind believers of the inseparable bond within the body of Christ and between God and His people. It also underscores the divine orchestration of events, where actions and outcomes are closely linked in God’s providential timing. Such insight encourages faith in God's perfect coordination and unity in His redemptive plan.
keyVerseReflection: In Matthew 13:29, Jesus says, 'Nay; lest while ye gather up the tares, ye root up also the wheat with them.' The use of ἅμα here, translated as 'also' or 'with,' highlights the risk of uprooting the wheat simultaneously with the tares. This word stresses the close association and simultaneous presence of both wheat and tares in the field, illustrating the care needed in judgment and the intertwined nature of good and evil until the proper time of separation.
